title: Symmetric Groups, Cycle Decomposition and the Sign Homomorphism

items.title: Support, fixed points, disjoint cycles, cycle length, disjoint-cycle decompositions, and cycle type
Cycles with disjoint supports commute
items.strategy: Check the composite at a point in the first support, the second support, and neither support; disjointness makes the other cycle fix the point in each nontrivial case.

items.title: Every permutation of a finite set is a product of pairwise disjoint cycles, uniquely up to reordering and cyclic rotation
items.strategy: Let the cyclic subgroup generated by the permutation act on the finite set. The non-singleton orbits give cycles by following successive powers; the orbit partition gives existence, and each cycle support must be one of those intrinsic orbits, giving uniqueness. Treat the identity as the empty product.

items.title: The order of a permutation is the least positive common multiple of its nontrivial cycle lengths, with value $1$ for the identity
items.strategy: Disjoint cycles commute, so a power of the permutation is the identity exactly when the same power fixes every cycle, equivalently when every cycle length divides the exponent; compare with the defining least positive exponent.

items.title: Every finite permutation is a product of transpositions, so the transpositions generate $S_n$
items.strategy: Verify the standard factorisation of a $k$-cycle as $(a_0\,a_{k-1})\cdots(a_0\,a_1)$, apply it to every factor in the disjoint-cycle decomposition, and retain the empty product for $n=0,1$ and the identity.

items.title: Inversions, inversion number, the sign $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)=(-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)}$, and even and odd permutations
Composing with a transposition reverses $(-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)}$
items.strategy: First swap adjacent positions and observe that exactly their mutual inversion toggles. Express a swap of positions $a<b$ as $2(b-a)-1$ adjacent swaps, an odd number, and track the factor $-1$.

items.title: Every transposition factorisation of $\sigma$ has parity $(-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)}$
items.strategy: Induct through a factorisation starting from the identity. Each transposition flips inversion sign, so a factorisation with $r$ factors has sign $(-1)^r$; hence any two factorisations of the same permutation have the same parity, including factorisations of the identity.

items.title: The sign is a homomorphism $S_n\to\{+1,-1\}$, surjective exactly when $n\ge 2$
items.strategy: Choose transposition factorisations of two permutations. Their concatenation factors the composite, so the well-defined parity theorem makes sign multiplicative. A transposition maps to $-1$ when $n\ge2$, while $S_0$ and $S_1$ are trivial and have image $\{1\}$.

items.title: A $k$-cycle has sign $(-1)^{k-1}$, and $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)=(-1)^{n-c(\sigma)}$ when fixed points are counted as cycles
items.strategy: Use the $k-1$ transpositions in the standard cycle factorisation, multiply signs across the disjoint-cycle decomposition, and sum $k_i-1$ over all cycles, including one-cycles.

items.title: The alternating group $A_n=\ker(\operatorname{sgn})$ of even permutations
$A_n$ is normal in $S_n$; for $n\ge2$, $2\,|A_n|=n!$, while $A_n=S_n$ for $n=0,1$
items.strategy: Normality follows from the kernel theorem. For $n\ge2$, multiplication by a fixed transposition bijects the even and odd fibres; their disjoint union is $S_n$, whose size is $n!$. Check the two trivial symmetric groups separately.

items.title: For $n\ge2$, sign is the unique nontrivial homomorphism $S_n\to\{+1,-1\}$
items.strategy: All transpositions are conjugate by an explicitly chosen permutation, so a homomorphism to the abelian two-element group has the same value on every transposition. Since transpositions generate, value $+1$ makes the map trivial and value $-1$ makes it sign.

title: Symmetric Groups and the Sign Homomorphism: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: From one-line notation to a disjoint-cycle decomposition, with the right-hand factor acting first
items.strategy: Compute the image table of an explicit product in $S_7$, follow each unused point until its orbit closes, and verify the recovered disjoint cycles pointwise.

items.title: Overlapping cycles need not commute
items.strategy: Evaluate $(0\,1)(1\,2)$ and $(1\,2)(0\,1)$ at $0$ in $S_3$; the images differ, isolating the disjoint-support hypothesis.

items.title: The six elements of $S_3$: one-line form, cycle structure, inversions, and sign
items.strategy: Enumerate the six bijections, compute each inversion set and disjoint-cycle form, and verify that the three even rows are exactly $A_3$.

items.title: Two different transposition factorisations of the same permutation have the same parity
items.strategy: Write a three-cycle with two transpositions and again with four by inserting a cancelling pair; compute both products and compare their parity with the inversion number.

items.title: A five-cycle is even and a six-cycle is odd
items.strategy: Expand each displayed cycle into the standard chain of transpositions and apply the cycle-sign formula, making the $k-1$ shift visible.

items.title: $A_4$ consists of the identity, eight $3$-cycles, and three products of disjoint transpositions
items.strategy: Classify the cycle types in $S_4$, apply the cycle-sign formula, enumerate the surviving permutations, and check the total $1+8+3=12=4!/2$.

items.title: $A_4$ has no subgroup of order $6$
items.strategy: A hypothetical order-six subgroup has index two and is normal. Since its six-element complement cannot contain all eight $3$-cycles, it contains one; normality and closure under inverses then force all eight $3$-cycles into it, a contradiction.

title: Matrices, the Matrix of a Linear Map, and Change of Basis

items.title: Rectangular matrix multiplication and the identity matrix $I_n$, including zero-sized shapes
Matrix multiplication is associative, unital, distributive, and compatible with scalar multiplication
items.strategy: Compare entries. Associativity interchanges the two finite summations and uses associativity and distributivity in the field; the identity, zero, distributive, and scalar laws follow from the same entry formula. Retain empty sums for every zero-sized intermediate dimension.

items.title: $M_n(F)$ is a ring under entrywise addition and matrix multiplication, including the zero ring $M_0(F)$
items.strategy: Combine the published vector-space addition with the matrix multiplication laws and check the ring axioms; for $n=0$ the unique empty matrix is both zero and identity, which the ring convention permits.

items.title: Matrix units $E_{ij}$ and the Kronecker delta
$E_{ij}E_{k\ell}=\delta_{jk}E_{i\ell}$
items.strategy: Evaluate the product entrywise: the finite sum has a nonzero term only at the common middle index, and that term exists exactly when $j=k$.

items.title: $M_n(F)$ is noncommutative for every $n\ge2$
items.strategy: Use $E_{01}E_{10}=E_{00}$ and $E_{10}E_{01}=E_{11}$ and distinguish the two matrices at entry $(0,0)$.

items.title: The transpose $A^{\mathsf T}$ of a matrix
Transpose is linear and involutive, and $(AB)^{\mathsf T}=B^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}$
items.strategy: The entrywise and involution claims are immediate from swapping indices. For products, expand the $(j,i)$ entry of $AB$ and compare it with the $(j,i)$ entry of the reversed product.

items.title: The space $\mathcal L(V,W)$ of linear maps with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication
$\mathcal L(V,W)$ is a vector space over the common scalar field
items.strategy: Show pointwise sums and scalar multiples remain linear, then inherit every vector-space axiom pointwise from $W$; include empty-domain and zero-space cases.

items.title: Invertible linear maps, linear isomorphisms, and inverse linear maps
Identity maps and composites of linear maps are linear
items.strategy: Substitute a general linear combination into the identity and composite, applying linearity first to the inner map and then to the outer map.

items.title: Coordinate columns $[v]_{\mathcal B}$ and matrices $[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}$ of linear maps relative to ordered bases
$[T(v)]_{\mathcal C}=[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}[v]_{\mathcal B}$
items.strategy: Expand $v$ in the domain basis, apply linearity, expand every image of a basis vector in the codomain basis, and identify each resulting coefficient with the corresponding row-by-column entry.

items.title: $T\mapsto[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}$ is a vector-space isomorphism $\mathcal L(V,W)\cong M_{m\times n}(F)$
items.strategy: Linearity follows columnwise. Injectivity follows because equality on a basis determines a linear map; for surjectivity, use the columns of an arbitrary matrix to prescribe images of the domain basis and extend by the unique-coordinate formula. Include $m=0$ and $n=0$.

items.title: $\dim_F M_{m\times n}(F)=mn$ and $\dim_F\mathcal L(V,W)=(\dim_FV)(\dim_FW)$ for finite-dimensional $V,W$
items.strategy: The $mn$ matrix units form an ordered basis of the matrix space, by reading one entry at a time. Transport that basis across the matrix-representation isomorphism and substitute the lengths of the chosen bases of $V$ and $W$, including either zero dimension.

items.title: $[S\circ T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal D}=[S]_{\mathcal C}^{\mathcal D}[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}$
items.strategy: Apply the coordinate-action theorem first to $T$ and then to $S$, use associativity of matrix multiplication, and identify the representing matrix by uniqueness or by evaluation on every basis column.

items.title: $\operatorname{End}_F(V)$ is a ring and matrix representation is a ring isomorphism $\operatorname{End}_F(V)\cong M_n(F)$
items.strategy: Use pointwise addition and composition on endomorphisms. The identity map is the multiplicative identity, composition distributes over addition, and the representation is already a bijective linear map that preserves composition and the identity matrix.

items.title: Invertible matrices and the general linear group $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$
A square matrix is invertible exactly when its multiplication map is a linear isomorphism; matrices preserve inverses of linear isomorphisms
items.strategy: An inverse matrix gives an inverse multiplication map. Conversely, represent the inverse linear map and use the composition formula to obtain both matrix inverse equations. Apply the same argument to an arbitrary finite-dimensional linear isomorphism in chosen bases.

items.title: Two finite-dimensional vector spaces over $F$ are linearly isomorphic if and only if they have the same dimension
items.strategy: An isomorphism sends a basis to a basis, so dimensions agree. Conversely, when the dimensions agree, send one ordered basis termwise to the other and extend by unique coordinates; the reverse basis assignment is its linear inverse, including dimension zero.

items.title: $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$ is a group under matrix multiplication, including the trivial group $\operatorname{GL}_0(F)$
items.strategy: Identify $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$ with the units of the ring $M_n(F)$ and apply the published units theorem; in the zero ring the sole empty matrix is its own inverse.

items.title: The change-of-basis matrix $P_{\mathcal C\leftarrow\mathcal B}=[\operatorname{id}_V]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}$
$[v]_{\mathcal C}=P_{\mathcal C\leftarrow\mathcal B}[v]_{\mathcal B}$ and $P_{\mathcal B\leftarrow\mathcal C}=P_{\mathcal C\leftarrow\mathcal B}^{-1}$
items.strategy: Apply coordinate action to the identity map for the coordinate formula, then represent the two identity compositions in both orders to obtain the two inverse equations. The empty-basis case gives the empty identity matrix.

items.title: $[T]_{\mathcal B'}^{\mathcal C'}=P_{\mathcal C'\leftarrow\mathcal C}[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}P_{\mathcal B\leftarrow\mathcal B'}$
items.strategy: Factor $T$ as the identity from the new codomain coordinates to the old codomain coordinates, followed by $T$ in the old bases, followed by the identity from the new domain basis to the old domain basis; apply the composition formula twice and check matrix shapes.

items.title: Similar matrices: $B=P^{-1}AP$ for an invertible $P$
Similarity is an equivalence relation, and two matrices represent the same endomorphism in two bases exactly when they are similar
items.strategy: Use $I$, $P^{-1}$, and products of conjugating matrices for reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity. The operator-to-matrix direction is the change-of-basis formula; conversely, use the columns of $P$ as a new ordered basis of $F^n$ and apply the same formula.

items.title: The trace $\operatorname{tr}(A)$ as the sum of the diagonal entries
Trace is a linear functional on $M_n(F)$
items.strategy: Apply entrywise addition and scalar multiplication on the diagonal and the finite-sum laws in the additive group of the field; the empty sum gives the unique map $M_0(F)\to F$ with value zero.

items.title: For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$, $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$
items.strategy: Expand both traces as the same finite double sum, commute the scalar factors in the field, and interchange the two finite index sets. The formula remains valid when either dimension is zero.

items.title: Similar matrices have the same trace
items.strategy: If $B=P^{-1}AP$, apply $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\operatorname{tr}(YX)$ to $X=P^{-1}A$ and $Y=P$, then simplify $PP^{-1}=I$.

items.title: The basis-independent trace of an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space

title: Matrices and Change of Basis: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A matrix represents a map $F^2\to F^3$ by its images of the standard basis vectors
items.strategy: Compute the two image columns, multiply the resulting $3$ by $2$ matrix by a general coordinate column, and recover the stated linear map.

items.title: The same operator has two different matrices in two ordered bases
items.strategy: Fix one explicit operator on $F^2$, compute its matrix in the standard basis and in a second displayed basis, compute the transition matrix, and verify the conjugation formula numerically. Keep the operator fixed throughout.

items.title: The quarter-turn $(x,y)\mapsto(-y,x)$ on $\mathbb R^2$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and square $-I_2$
items.strategy: Apply the map to the two standard basis vectors, assemble the columns, multiply the matrix by itself, and interpret the square as the half-turn.

items.title: Two explicit $2$ by $2$ matrices do not commute
items.strategy: Use $E_{01}$ and $E_{10}$, compute both products, and display the different diagonal results.

items.title: A nonzero square-zero matrix is not similar to any diagonal matrix
items.strategy: Take $N=E_{01}$ in $M_2(F)$. If $N=P^{-1}DP$ with $D$ diagonal, then $0=N^2=P^{-1}D^2P$, so every diagonal entry of $D$ squares to zero and hence is zero in a field; this would force $N=0$.

items.title: Changing both domain and codomain bases of a map $F^2\to F^3$ uses both sides of the formula
items.strategy: Choose explicit old and new bases in both spaces, compute the two transition matrices and the old matrix of the map, multiply in the prescribed order, and independently recompute the new matrix from images of new basis vectors.

items.title: A $2$ by $3$ matrix and a $3$ by $2$ matrix give square products of different sizes but equal traces
items.strategy: Multiply one explicit pair in both orders, display the resulting $2$ by $2$ and $3$ by $3$ matrices, and compare their diagonal sums.
